DESCRIPTION: The probabilistic-feasibility extension is not wired into the actual allocation path. `_solve_greedy()` and `solve()` allocate purely against deterministic `L`, while `feasibility_probability()` / `dispatch_check()` exist only as an optional side helper and are never consulted by `DynamicManager.get_allocation()`. I reproduced a one-model case with `L=10000`, `L_std=4000`, `task_load=9500`: `solve()` returned `alloc_matrix [[1]]`, but `dispatch_check()` on the same model returned `(False, 0.5497382248301129)`. So the advertised timeout-risk guard cannot actually stop risky dispatches.

DESCRIPTION: `process_round()` performs no integrity checks tying `responses`, `findings`, active models, or embedded round numbers to the manager’s actual round. It trusts caller-supplied `Finding.model_id` and `Finding.round_idx`, then feeds the findings straight into convergence and diminishing-returns state. I reproduced a round with only `m1` responding but a finding `Finding('f1', 'ghost', 99, ...)`; `process_round()` accepted it, stored `['ghost']` in the round result, and `get_cumulative_classes(0)` became `1`. That lets unknown, excluded, or future-stamped findings poison convergence, yield, and audit history without any rejection.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

DESCRIPTION: Hard-feasibility failures are warning-only at the public API boundary. `_check_feasibility()` can detect F1/F3 violations, but `solve()` still returns a normal `(Allocation, cost, balanced)` tuple and `DynamicManager.get_allocation()` forwards it unchanged; there is no boolean or exception the caller can reliably branch on. I reproduced a single-model case with `L=1000` and a `2000`-token task: `solve()` returned `alloc_matrix [[1]]` and `balanced=True`, with only a `UserWarning`. In a non-interactive orchestrator that is easy to miss, so impossible plans can be dispatched as if valid.

DESCRIPTION: Failure handling’s underperformance baseline is frozen to the initial fingerprints and never follows the live adaptive state. `FailureHandler` snapshots `self.models` in `__init__`, and `_expected_performance()` always reads `model.fingerprint` from that frozen dict, while `DynamicManager.update_fingerprints()` only updates `_live_fingerprints`. I verified this by mutating `mgr._live_fingerprints['m2']` from `(0.2, 0.8, 0.8, 0.8)` to `(0.9, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)`: `_expected_performance('m2')` stayed `0.71` before and after. So the adaptive loop is also severed in Area 6, not just in allocation/reassignment.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

DESCRIPTION: Degraded two-model mode still preserves a dedicated `COL`, even though initial assignment only creates a `COL` when the pool size is at least three. `reassign()` decides whether a `COL` slot exists from `len(self._models)` (original pool), not from the current active pool. I reproduced a 3-model system degraded to active `{'m1','m2'}` and `reassign()` returned `{'m1': PM, 'm2': COL}`. That changes the degraded-mode role semantics and also feeds the wrong role baseline into failure handling precisely when the system is already under stress.

DESCRIPTION: The system assumes identifier uniqueness but never validates it, and duplicate IDs silently collapse state. I reproduced three input models `['dup', 'dup', 'other']`; after construction, `role_map`, `capability_scores`, and `FailureHandler.models` all retained only `['dup', 'other']`. Because many subsystems key by `model_id` and `Allocation` later resolves by `list.index()`, duplicate model or task IDs can silently drop entities or alias them to the wrong row/column instead of failing fast.
